title: Console walkthrough: usage analytics & cost breakdown - Cascade Retail
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Cascade Retail through the Console usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and a detailed cost breakdown. Key topics: token-level cost attribution, per-route latency and error dashboards, route-level caching and batching recommendations, dedicated vs hosted capacity tradeoffs, and compliance (SOC 2, SSO/KMS). Customer requested pricing worksheet, SOC 2 artifact, and a pilot to run 1 week of traffic to assess cost and latency on a 10M token/month baseline.
next_steps: Alex Monroe: send pricing worksheet and dedicated capacity options (due 2026-07-16)
Jordan Park: share quickstart guide and sample dashboard export (due 2026-07-15)
Cascade: confirm pilot traffic window and provide sample prompt mix (due 2026-07-20)
Schedule pilot kickoff call week of 2026-07-20
action_items: Alex Monroe: send pricing, dedicated capacity worksheet, and relevant case studies (2026-07-16)
Jordan Park: share SOC 2 summary and console dashboard export (2026-07-15)
Samir Patel: provide sample anonymized prompt set and expected throughput numbers (2026-07-20)
Ethan Wu: confirm outbound IP allowlist for pilot (2026-07-18)
meeting_header: Date: 2026-07-14 | Time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Cascade), Lina Torres (Cascade), Ethan Wu (Cascade)
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Alex Monroe, AE on the account. Jordan's our SE, he'll do the console walkthrough. Samir, Lina, Ethan, thanks for making time.
[00:12] Samir (Cascade): Yeah thanks Alex. We've been looking forward to this. We've seen your docs but want to see the real per-route cost breakdown and how we can correlate costs to our product routes.
[00:25] Jordan (Redwood SE): Cool, I'll share my screen in a sec. High level we'll cover usage analytics, per-route dashboards, cost attribution down to tokens, and a few recommendations for batching and prefix caching.
[00:38] Lina (Cascade): Quick context, we run customer support summarization and a recommendations assistant. Roughly 10M tokens / month now, peak concurrency 200 RPS, latency target is sub-300ms for the recommendation route.
[00:52] Ethan (Cascade): And from infra we care about predictable cost and IP restrictions - want private networking if possible.
[01:05] Jordan (SE): Understood. First slide - the Console overview. The usage analytics page gives you time-series of tokens, requests, errors, and latency by model and by route. You can pivot to any route - so for your support-summary route you could see avg tokens per request and token cost contribution.
[01:28] Alex (AE): One thing customers like is the per-route cost share. It shows what percent of total spend each route contributes, and you can drill into token type (input vs output).
[01:40] Samir: How accurate is the token attribution? If we rerun prompts with slightly different tokenizers we need to reconcile.
[01:48] Jordan: Good question. We use model runtime tokenization counts - it's runtime-accurate, but if you pre-process differently the numbers can differ. We provide a tokenization snapshot export so you can reconcile. There is occasional mismatch when folks post-process or trim whitespace, but we call that out in the export.
[02:05] [Jordan screenshares console]
[02:20] Jordan: Here's the per-route dashboard. Top panel: throughput and latency. Middle: token breakdown and cost. Bottom: errors and top failing prompts. See this spike around 10:30 where latency jumped - you can click into trace to see request-level logs.
[02:40] Lina: That error trace - is that from our sandbox traffic or could it be infra?
[02:48] Jordan: It shows the model fell back to a slower variant during capacity pressure - our routing policy allowed fallback to keep successful responses but with higher latency. You can set stricter routing to avoid fallbacks if you'd rather error than degrade latency.
[03:05] Alex: That's an important tradeoff - many customers prefer graceful degradation, but you can choose strict SLO enforcement.
[03:15] Ethan: About private networking - can we pin to VPC or do you require outbound to public endpoints?
[03:23] Jordan: For Private deployments we give a customer-managed control plane and VPC peering. For Hosted you can use IP allowlisting and dedicated capacity to reduce cross-tenant interference. We also support on-prem package for fully air-gapped.
[03:40] Samir: So for a pilot we could start on Hosted with dedicated capacity and then move to Private if compliance needs it?
[03:47] Alex: Exactly. Many customers prototype on hosted dedicated, then transition to Private for production.
[03:55] [05:00] Jordan: Cost breakdown view - here's token price per model variant multiplied by captured tokens. Notice we separate inference compute, model variant surcharge, and console/observability charges. You can get a per-route line item CSV for billing.
[05:20] Lina: Do you show amortized GPU hours or just token-level cost?
[05:27] Jordan: We show both. Token-level for immediate attribution, and an amortized compute view for reserved/dedicated pools - that helps with cost forecasting if you're on committed capacity.
[05:40] Samir: On amortized compute - if we hit a different sequence length distribution in production, will that skew the amortized numbers?
[05:50] Jordan: It can. That's why Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and batching profiles based on your observed seq-len histogram. We recommend a short exploratory window to gather representative distribution before sizing reserved capacity.
[06:05] Alex: We'll include a sample worksheet for that.
[06:10] [06:30] Jordan: Now, look at route-level caching - prefix/KV cache coverage. For your support-summary route, you might get high cache hit rates for repeated templates, which dramatically lowers per-token cost. This panel estimates cost saved from current cache hits and suggests keys to add to increase hit rate.
[06:52] Lina: That's interesting - how does the cache handle PII? We can't cache customer messages in plaintext.
[07:00] Jordan: You can configure the cache to hash or redact PII before storing, or disable caching for routes with sensitive data. The console flags routes with PII risk and lets you opt out. We'll also show audit logs of cache hits for compliance.
[07:20] Ethan: Audit logs - retention and export? We need 12 months for our audits.
[07:28] Alex: We offer add-on longer retention for observability exports. Jordan will share the retention tiers and pricing.
[07:36] [08:00] Samir: On security - SOC 2, SAML support, and KMS integration are must-haves.
[08:08] Jordan: We are SOC 2 Type II. We support SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning and customer KMS/HSM for private deployments. For hosted, we can integrate with customer KMS in dedicated/private deployments. I'll attach the SOC 2 summary.
[08:28] Lina: Great. Also, we're concerned about cold-start latency with the recommendation model - does Redwood warm kernels or keep KV cache hot?
[08:38] Jordan: For dedicated pools we support pre-warming and kernel persistence. We also run continuous batching and reuse KV cache across requests when appropriate. For strict latency SLOs you can pin model variants to avoid cold starts.
[09:00] Alex: Quick demo: switching to the cost breakdown CSV export, you can filter to just the recommend route and group by model variant. It shows total tokens, input vs output, and a computed cost column.
[09:20] [09:40] Samir: The cost numbers - do they include downstream embeddings or just generation?
[09:47] Jordan: They include all model invocations captured by the route - so if you call embeddings or rerankers from that route, they appear as separate line items.
[10:00] Lina: Any visibility into per-customer or tenant-level attribution? We have multi-tenant customers and want to bill them back.
[10:09] Jordan: Yes, if you pass through tenant metadata in headers we surface tenant-level attribution and you can generate billing reports. We'll give the header conventions in the quickstart.
[10:22] Ethan: For pilot - what's the typical timeline and what do you need from us?
[10:30] Alex: Typical pilot is 1-2 weeks of mirrored traffic or a slice of production; Jordan will need sample prompt mix, expected tokens per request, concurrency profile, and any IP allowlist. We'll run benchmarks and provide a recommended config and cost projection.
[10:48] Samir: We can do a 1-week mirrored pilot of about 2M tokens to start.
[10:55] Jordan: Perfect. We'll instrument so you can see the console metrics and cost delta.
[11:05] [11:30] Jordan: Now some notes on Optimize recommendations - the console flags suggested batch sizes and quantization profiles per model and gives an expected percent reduction in cost and impact on latency. Example: quantize to int8 for the recommendation model, expected cost cut 35% with minimal latency change for your median seq-len.
[11:55] Lina: Do you run regression tests on quality after quantization?
[12:02] Jordan: Yes - Optimize ties to prompt sets/evals. We run a small eval set and report any regressions. If quality drops we backfill alerts and can revert.
[12:20] [12:40] Samir: Are there any vendor lock-in concerns with your rollouts or data portability?
[12:47] Alex: We focus on portability - you can pin model versions and export configs. The console exports full routing and batching configuration as YAML for reproducibility.
[13:05] Ethan: What about pricing - dedicated pools vs pay-as-you-go hosted?
[13:12] Alex: Dedicated is committed monthly with lower unit costs and predictable throughput. Hosted pay-as-you-go has higher per-token but no commit. We'll send a side-by-side worksheet for your expected volume.
[13:30] Lina: Also send examples of customers who moved from hosted to private and the migration process.
[13:36] Alex: Will do. We have a case study with a retail customer that migrated to Private for data residency.
[13:45] [14:00] Jordan: A couple more console features - anomaly detection on spend, route-level alerts, SLA-based automated fallbacks and canary rollouts. You can configure a canary for a new model variant at 5% then ramp to 50% then 100% with auto-rollback on quality regression.
[14:25] Samir: That rollback is important; we can't afford regressions in production.
[14:30] Jordan: Exactly. The console hooks to your eval sets to automatically detect regressions and rollback.
[14:40] [15:00] Alex: Recap - action items: we'll send pricing worksheet, SOC 2 summary, sample dashboard export, and the quickstart. Cascade will provide pilot traffic and tenant header conventions.
[15:12] Lina: Sounds good. Any remaining questions from Cascade?
[15:18] Ethan: One more - does Redwood support customer-managed logging for audit compliance?
[15:24] Jordan: For Private or Dedicated we can stream logs to your storage via secure connector; for hosted, we offer a secure export and longer retention add-on.
[15:36] Samir: Great. We'll get the pilot details to you by next week.
[15:42] Alex: Thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[15:46] Lina: Thanks, bye.
[15:48] [END]
